questions.question: Two loudspeakers driven by one signal generator (160 Hz) are in phase. Explain why students hear a loud sound at point O.
questions.answer: Waves from both speakers arrive at O in phase (path difference is a whole number of wavelengths), so they reinforce: constructive interference.
steps: Both loudspeakers are driven by the same signal generator, so they are coherent and emit in phase.
At O the path lengths from the two speakers differ by a whole number of wavelengths (including zero).
Waves arriving with zero phase difference superpose, so their displacements add.
The resultant amplitude is a maximum, so the sound is loud at O.

questions.question: Loudspeakers at 3.00 m from line XY (160 Hz) give a minimum 84 cm from O. Determine the speed of sound.
questions.answer: Speed of sound = 3.4 x 10^2 m s^-1 (about 340 m s^-1).
steps: The loudspeakers are 5.00 m apart and 3.00 m from XY, with O on the line midway between them, so each is 2.50 m from the axis through O.
The first minimum is 0.84 m from O, so the distances from the point to the speakers are s1 = sqrt(3.00^2 + (2.50 - 0.84)^2) = 3.43 m and s2 = sqrt(3.00^2 + (2.50 + 0.84)^2) = 4.49 m.
Path difference = 4.49 - 3.43 = 1.06 m.
The first minimum (antiphase, destructive) has path difference = lambda / 2, so lambda = 2 x 1.06 = 2.12 m.
v = f x lambda = 160 Hz x 2.12 m = 339 m s^-1, about 3.4 x 10^2 m s^-1.

questions.question: Explain one reason why a microphone connected to an oscilloscope gives much less uncertainty than students walking along XY.
questions.answer: The microphone and oscilloscope locate the amplitude minimum objectively, removing the subjective judgement of human hearing.
steps: Human hearing judges loudness subjectively and cannot reliably pinpoint the exact quiet position.
A microphone converts the sound into an electrical signal whose size depends on the pressure amplitude.
The oscilloscope displays this signal, so the amplitude can be read precisely at each position.
The position of minimum amplitude is therefore found with much less uncertainty.

questions.question: A student suggests the speed of sound experiment gives equally valid results in a classroom. Criticise this suggestion.
questions.answer: Sound reflects off walls, ceiling and floor, so reflected waves superpose with the direct waves and blur the loud and quiet zones.
steps: Sound reflects from walls, the ceiling and the floor of a classroom.
Reflected waves travel different path lengths and superpose with the direct waves.
This changes the pattern of loud and quiet zones, so the minimum positions no longer match the direct-wave geometry.
The results are therefore unreliable; an open space avoids these reflections.

questions.question: The diagram shows how the displacement varies with distance along a stationary wave at two instants of time (X is on the first loop; Y and Z are on the second loop, Z at the antinode). Which statement is not correct? A Points X and Z are in antiphase with each other. B Points Y and Z have the same amplitude of vibration. C Points Y and Z have the same frequency of vibration. D Point Z is an antinode.
questions.answer: B: Y and Z do not have the same amplitude, so this statement is not correct.
steps: In a stationary wave the amplitude depends on position: it is zero at a node and a maximum at an antinode.
Z is at the peak of the loop (an antinode), but Y is part-way between the node and the antinode, so its amplitude is smaller than Z's. B is false.
A is true: X and Z are on adjacent loops, which vibrate in antiphase.
C is true: every point on a stationary wave vibrates at the same frequency. D is true: Z is at maximum amplitude.

questions.question: Laser light through a diffraction grating. Which change would increase the distance between adjacent maxima? A decrease grating-screen distance; B decrease distance between grating lines; C decrease intensity; D decrease wavelength.
questions.answer: B - decreasing the distance between the lines (d) increases the spacing of the maxima.
steps: Spacing of adjacent maxima on the screen is x = lambda D / d, where D is grating-screen distance and d is line spacing.
Option A decreases D, so x decreases.
Option B decreases d (lines closer together), so x increases: this is correct.
Option C changes brightness only, not the position of the maxima.
Option D decreases lambda, so x decreases.

questions.question: Two waves from the same source travel along different paths and then meet at a point P. The phase difference between the waves at P is 1.5 pi radians. Which is a possible path difference? A 3 lambda/2; B 7 lambda/4; C 3 lambda; D 7 lambda/2.
questions.answer: B: 7 lambda / 4.
steps: Phase difference = 2 pi x (path difference / lambda), so path difference = (1.5 pi / 2 pi) lambda = 3 lambda / 4, or 3 lambda / 4 plus any whole number of wavelengths.
B: 7 lambda / 4 = 3 lambda / 4 + lambda, which gives a phase difference of 3.5 pi, equivalent to 1.5 pi.
A gives 3 pi, C gives 6 pi and D gives 7 pi, none equivalent to 1.5 pi.

questions.question: Which is a correct description of how to use laser light and a diffraction grating with n = d sin theta? A angle measured by protractor; B grating parallel to beam; C grating parallel to screen; D spacing measured with micrometer.
questions.answer: C - the grating is set parallel to the screen so the grating-screen distance is uniform.
steps: The equation n lambda = d sin theta needs the angle of each maximum, found from distances measured on the screen, not with a protractor (A is wrong).
The grating must face the beam, so it is perpendicular to the beam, not parallel to it (B is wrong).
The grating must be parallel to the screen so that the grating-screen distance is the same across the grating (C is correct).
Distances between dots are measured with a metre rule, not a micrometer (D is wrong).

questions.question: Using Huygens construction, explain how diffraction occurs as laser light passes through a small circular gap.
questions.answer: Each point of the wavefront at the gap acts as a source of secondary wavelets, which spread into the region behind the gap so the wave bends round the edge.
steps: Huygens: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets.
At the gap only the wavefront points inside the opening pass the wave through.
The secondary wavelets spread out into the region behind the gap, forming a new, curved wavefront.
Diffraction is significant when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

questions.question: Sketch a graph of intensity along line AB across the circular-gap diffraction pattern.
questions.answer: A symmetrical graph with a tall central maximum in the middle of AB and weaker, equally spaced outer maxima whose heights decrease away from the centre, with zero intensity between them.
steps: Label the centre of AB as the point of greatest intensity: a tall peak well above all the others.
On each side the intensity drops to about zero (dark ring) and then rises to a much smaller secondary maximum.
Each further secondary maximum is lower than the one before, so the peaks decrease in height outwards.
The pattern is symmetrical about the centre, and the central peak is the widest (about twice the width of the outer peaks).

questions.question: A string of length L = 1.70 m vibrates in the stationary wave pattern shown. Determine the wavelength.
questions.answer: Wavelength = 0.85 m.
steps: The pattern between P and Q has 4 loops, and each loop is half a wavelength.
So L = 4 x (lambda / 2) = 2 lambda.

questions.question: A hanging mass m = 0.20 kg stretches a string with mass per unit length 4.5 x 10^-3 kg m-1. Calculate the speed of waves on the string.
questions.answer: Speed = 20.9 m s-1 (about 21 m s-1).
steps: The tension is provided by the hanging mass: T = mg = 0.20 x 9.81 = 1.96 N.
Wave speed on a stretched string is v = sqrt(T / mu), where mu is the mass per unit length.

questions.question: The vibration generator frequency is reduced to give a different standing wave. Explain the effect on the speed of the waves on the string.
questions.answer: No effect: wave speed depends only on tension and mass per unit length, not on frequency; the wavelength increases instead.
steps: Wave speed on a string is set by the tension and the mass per unit length: v = sqrt(T / mu).
Lowering the generator frequency does not change the tension or mu.
Since v = f lambda and v is constant, a lower frequency gives a longer wavelength.
So the speed of the waves on the string stays the same.

questions.question: Two waves, of wavelength lambda, from a single source diverge and then meet again. Which situation would cause constructive interference? A a path difference of lambda/2; B a path difference of lambda; C a phase difference of pi/2; D a phase difference of pi.
questions.answer: B: a path difference of lambda.
steps: Constructive interference needs the waves in phase: a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths (phase difference 0, 2 pi, 4 pi ...).
B: a path difference of lambda is a phase difference of 2 pi, so the waves reinforce.
A (lambda/2) gives a phase difference of pi, and D (pi) is antiphase, so these give destructive interference. C (pi/2) gives partial reinforcement only.

questions.question: Two waves from the same source arrive at a point with a path difference of 3 lambda/8, where lambda is the wavelength. Which is the phase difference? A 34 deg; B 68 deg; C 135 deg; D 270 deg.
questions.answer: C: 135 deg.
steps: Phase difference = 360 deg x (path difference / lambda).
Phase difference = 360 deg x 3/8 = 135 deg.
This matches option C.

questions.question: A diffraction grating has 300 lines per mm. Laser light directed at it gives a first order maximum on a screen 2.00 m from the grating and 0.40 m from the central maximum (see diagram). Which calculation gives the wavelength, in mm? A 300 sin(theta), theta = sin^-1(0.40/2.00); B 300 sin(theta), theta = tan^-1(0.40/2.00); C sin(theta)/300, theta = sin^-1(0.40/2.00); D sin(theta)/300, theta = tan^-1(0.40/2.00).
questions.answer: D: wavelength = sin(theta) / 300 mm, where theta = tan^-1(0.40 / 2.00).
steps: The line spacing is d = 1/300 mm, so lambda = d sin theta = sin theta / 300 (in mm). This rules out A and B.
The 2.00 m is the perpendicular distance from the grating to the screen and 0.40 m is the sideways distance, so tan theta = 0.40/2.00.
The ray itself is longer than 2.00 m, so sin theta is not 0.40/2.00, which rules out C.
Check: theta = 11.3 deg, so lambda = sin 11.3 deg / 300 = 6.5 x 10^-4 mm = 650 nm, a sensible visible wavelength.

questions.question: Which change would increase the speed of waves along a vibrating string? A increase frequency; B increase length; C increase mass per unit length; D increase tension.
questions.answer: D - increasing the tension increases the speed, since v = sqrt(T / mu).
steps: The speed of waves on a string is v = sqrt(T / mu).
Frequency and length do not appear in this formula, so changing them does not change v (A and B are wrong).
Increasing mass per unit length mu reduces v (C is wrong).
Increasing the tension T increases v (D is correct).

questions.question: Two waves leave a source in phase with wavelength 8.0 cm. Which gives constructive interference? A path difference 16.0 cm; B path difference (symbol missing); C phase difference 180 deg; D phase difference 3 rad.
questions.answer: A - a path difference of 16.0 cm, which is two wavelengths.
steps: Constructive interference needs a path difference that is a whole number of wavelengths.
16.0 cm / 8.0 cm = 2.0 wavelengths, a whole number, so the waves reinforce (A).
A phase difference of 180 deg gives destructive interference (C is wrong).
3 rad is about 172 deg, which is not 0 or 360 deg, so it is not constructive (D is wrong).

questions.question: Wavefronts approach gaps of different sizes. In which diagram are the diffracted wavefronts not semicircular?
questions.answer: B: the gap is much wider than the wavelength, so the diffracted wavefronts are not semicircular.
steps: Diffracted wavefronts are semicircular only when the gap is about the size of the wavelength or smaller.
In A the wavefront spacing is about equal to the gap width, and C has a gap narrower than the wavelength, so both spread out in semicircles.
In D the gap is only about 1.5 wavelengths, so the spreading is still pronounced.
In B the wavefronts are close together (small wavelength) and the gap is about 4 wavelengths wide, so most of the wavefront passes straight through and little diffraction occurs except at the edges.

questions.question: The speed of waves on a vibrating string is investigated using the apparatus shown. Length of string between vibrator and pulley = L; length of string between pulley and hanging masses = L/3; mass of whole string = m; mass of hanging masses = M. Which expression represents the speed of the waves on the string? A sqrt(4MgL/(3m)); B sqrt(2MgL/(3m)); C sqrt(MgL/m); D sqrt(MgL/(3m)).
questions.answer: A: v = sqrt(4MgL / (3m)).
steps: Tension in the string T = Mg (weight of the hanging masses).
The whole string has length L + L/3 = 4L/3 and mass m, so mass per unit length mu = m / (4L/3) = 3m / (4L).
v = sqrt(T / mu) = sqrt(Mg x 4L / (3m)) = sqrt(4MgL / (3m)).

questions.question: Two in-phase sources S1 and S2 in a ripple tank. Explain the type of superposition at positions A and B on the diagram of crests.
questions.answer: A: constructive superposition (waves arrive in phase). B: destructive superposition (waves arrive in antiphase).
steps: S1 and S2 are in phase and emit waves of the same wavelength, so the waves are coherent and superpose at every point.

A is about 3.5 wavelengths from S1 and 4.5 wavelengths from S2: path difference of about one wavelength, so the waves arrive in phase (here both are at a trough). Displacements add, giving constructive interference and a large amplitude.
B lies on a crest line from S2 (about 5 wavelengths away) but is about 3.5 wavelengths from S1, where there is a trough: path difference of about 1.5 wavelengths, so the waves arrive in antiphase.
At B a crest meets a trough, so the displacements cancel: destructive interference and a very small amplitude.

questions.question: A microwave oven has a source that emits microwaves in all directions into the oven. The diagram shows the paths of two microwave rays that meet at point L. The interference between the waves following these two paths could cause heating effects at L depending on the wavelength. Which row is possible at L? A maximum heating, wavelength 24 cm; B maximum heating, wavelength 18 cm; C no heating, wavelength 24 cm; D no heating, wavelength 18 cm.
questions.answer: C: no heating with a wavelength of 24 cm.
steps: Path 1 = 22 + 8 = 30 cm and path 2 = 15 + 27 = 42 cm, so the path difference is 12 cm.
For a wavelength of 24 cm, 12 cm = lambda / 2, so the waves arrive in antiphase and cancel: no heating.

For a wavelength of 18 cm, 12 cm = 2/3 lambda, which is neither a whole number of wavelengths nor an odd number of half wavelengths, so neither maximum heating nor zero heating occurs. Only row C is possible.

questions.question: A sound wave travels through air. The diagram represents the displacement of air particles along the wave at an instant in time (V at the start, W the maximum, X the zero crossing, Y the minimum, Z the end of one cycle). There is a compression at position V. At which position is there also a compression? A W; B X; C Y; D Z.
questions.answer: D: Z.
steps: Compressions and rarefactions occur at the points of zero displacement, where neighbouring particles are displaced towards or away from each other.
V and Z both have zero displacement and the same gradient, and they are one whole wavelength apart, so they are in the same state: both compressions.
X also has zero displacement but the opposite gradient, so it is a rarefaction. W and Y are at maximum displacement, where the air density is normal.

questions.question: A student finds the wavelength of laser light with a laser, grating and screen. Which measurement is not required? A grating-to-screen distance; B central maximum to first order distance; C laser-to-grating distance; D slit spacing of the grating.
questions.answer: C - the laser-to-grating distance; it does not appear in the working equation.
steps: The working equation is lambda = d x / L, or n lambda = d sin theta.
The grating-to-screen distance L (option A) is needed.
The distance x from the central maximum to the first order (option B) is needed.
The slit spacing d (option D) is known from the grating label, so it is needed as a value.
The laser-to-grating distance does not appear in the equation, so it is not required (C).

questions.question: The diagram shows how the displacement varies with distance along a stationary wave at two instants of time (W and X are on the first loop, either side of its peak; Y and Z are on the second loop). Which statement is correct? A Points W and X are in antiphase. B Points W and Y are in phase. C Points X and Y are in phase. D Points X and Z are in antiphase.
questions.answer: D: points X and Z are in antiphase.
steps: In a stationary wave, all points between two adjacent nodes vibrate in phase, and points in adjacent loops vibrate in antiphase.
W and X are on the same loop, so they are in phase (A is wrong).
Y and Z are on the next loop, so they are in antiphase with W and X (B and C are wrong).
X is on loop 1 and Z is on loop 2, so they are in antiphase (D is correct).

questions.question: A grating has 450 lines per mm. The first bright dot X is at a measured position on the screen. Determine the wavelength of the laser light.
questions.answer: Wavelength = 6.3 x 10^-7 m (630 nm).
steps: Line spacing d = 1 / (450 x 10^3 lines per m) = 2.22 x 10^-6 m.
X is the first order maximum (n = 1): tan theta = 0.500 / 1.690, so theta = 16.5 deg.
lambda = d sin theta / n = 2.22 x 10^-6 x sin 16.5 deg = 2.22 x 10^-6 x 0.2837.
lambda = 6.30 x 10^-7 m = 630 nm.

questions.question: Explain why a series of bright dots is seen on the screen when the laser is switched on.
questions.answer: Coherent laser light diffracted by the grating interferes constructively only at angles where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, giving bright maxima.
steps: Laser light is monochromatic and coherent, so the waves from all the lines are in phase at the grating.
Each line diffracts the light into many directions.
Waves from neighbouring lines meet with path difference n lambda, which is constructive.
This happens only at angles given by d sin theta = n lambda, producing bright maxima.
At other angles the waves cancel, so dark background shows between the bright dots.

questions.question: The laser is replaced by a parallel beam of white light. Suggest what is now observed on the screen.
questions.answer: A white central maximum with coloured spectra on each side, with violet nearest the centre and red furthest away.
steps: Each wavelength has its own maxima at angles given by sin theta = n lambda / d.
Zero path difference applies to all wavelengths at the centre, so the central maximum is white.
On either side, the maxima of different colours spread out into a spectrum.
Violet has the shortest wavelength, so its angle is smallest and it lies closest to the centre; red is furthest.

questions.question: The metre rule has resolution 1 mm, but distances were recorded to the nearest 0.5 cm. Suggest why.
questions.answer: The nodes on the string are not sharply defined, so their positions can only be judged to about 0.5 cm, not to 1 mm.
steps: The metre rule can resolve 1 mm, so its resolution is not the limit.
The string blurs over a region near each node, so there is no sharp point to read.
The uncertainty in judging the node position is therefore about 0.5 cm.
Recording to a finer resolution would not improve the true precision.

questions.question: Using the graph of d against 1/f and mass per unit length 4.5 x 10^-4 kg m-1, determine the total mass of the hanging masses.
questions.answer: Total mass of hanging masses = 0.20 kg.
steps: d is half a wavelength, so lambda = 2d and v = f lambda = 2fd, giving d = (v / 2)(1/f). The gradient of the d against 1/f graph is v / 2.
Gradient of the best-fit line = 2.4 m / 0.072 s = 33 m s^-1 (point (0.072, 2.4) lies on the line).
The tension equals the weight of the hanging masses, so M = T / g = 2.0 / 9.81 = 0.20 kg.

questions.question: The string is replaced by one with twice the mass per unit length, other quantities unchanged. Add a line to the graph of d against 1/f for the new string.
questions.answer: A straight line through the origin with a gradient about 24 m s^-1, lower than the original 33 m s^-1 line (about 0.71 times as steep).
steps: With the same tension and twice the mass per unit length, v = sqrt(T / mu) falls by a factor of sqrt(2).
The gradient v / 2 falls from about 33 to 33 / sqrt(2) = 23.5 m s^-1.
The new line is still straight and passes through the origin, but is below the original line.
For example it passes through d = 1.4 m at 1/f = 0.060 s and d = 1.9 m at 1/f = 0.080 s.

questions.question: Laser light is incident on a grating at 90 deg, with angle theta1 = 14.0 deg shown on the diagram. Calculate angle theta2.
questions.answer: theta2 = 28.9 deg.
steps: theta1 is the angle of the n = 1 maximum and theta2 (measured from the central line) is the angle of the n = 2 maximum.
d sin theta1 = lambda and d sin theta2 = 2 lambda, so sin theta2 = 2 sin theta1.
sin theta2 = 2 x sin 14.0 deg = 2 x 0.2419 = 0.4838.

questions.question: The angles of maxima for n = 1 to 4 are measured. Describe a graphical method to find the wavelength, with grating spacing d known.
questions.answer: Plot sin theta against n; the best-fit straight line through the origin has gradient lambda / d, so lambda = gradient x d.
steps: For a maximum of order n, the grating equation is n lambda = d sin theta.
Rearranged, sin theta = (lambda / d) n, which is a straight line through the origin.
Plot sin theta on the y-axis against n on the x-axis for n = 1 to 4, and draw the best-fit line.
Find the gradient of the line; gradient = lambda / d.
Wavelength lambda = gradient x d.

questions.question: Grating labelled 300 lines per mm. The distance on the screen from n = 0 to n = 2 is 0.397 m, screen distance 2.00 m, wavelength 650 nm. Deduce whether the label is correct.
questions.answer: Incorrect: the data give about 150 lines per mm (d about 6.7 micrometres), not 300 lines per mm.
steps: For the second order, 2 lambda = d sin theta.
From geometry, tan theta = x / L = 0.397 / 2.00 = 0.1985, so theta = 11.2 deg.
sin theta = 0.1947.
d = 2 x 650 x 10^-9 / 0.1947 = 6.7 x 10^-6 m, so 1 / d is about 150 lines per mm.
300 lines per mm would give d = 3.3 micrometres, so the label is incorrect.

questions.question: Sounds of 880 Hz and 882 Hz are produced. The ear hears frequencies differing by less than 0.3 percent as the same. Show that they are heard as the same frequency.
questions.answer: The difference of 2 Hz is 0.23 percent of 880 Hz, less than 0.3 percent, so they are heard as one frequency.
steps: Frequency difference = 882 Hz - 880 Hz = 2 Hz.
Percentage difference = 2 / 880 x 100 = 0.227 percent.
0.227 percent is less than the 0.3 percent threshold, so the ear cannot resolve the two frequencies.
Therefore the sounds are heard as the same frequency.

questions.question: When 880 Hz and 882 Hz are heard together, loudness rises and falls repeatedly. Explain why, referring to coherence and phase difference.
questions.answer: The two sources differ slightly in frequency, so they are not coherent: their phase difference changes steadily, so they reinforce and cancel in turn, giving beats at 2 Hz.
steps: The two sounds differ in frequency by 2 Hz, so their phase difference is not constant; they are not coherent.
The phase difference between the two waves at the ear changes steadily with time.
When the waves are in phase they superpose constructively, giving a loud sound.
When they are in antiphase they superpose destructively, giving a quiet sound.
The loudness therefore varies at the beat frequency f1 - f2 = 2 Hz.
Loud maxima occur twice every second.

questions.question: A wire of length 18.7 cm (fixed at both ends, fundamental) has mu = 5.08 x 10^-3 kg m-1 and gives 882 Hz. Tension is adjusted to give 880 Hz. Calculate the decrease in tension.
questions.answer: Decrease in tension = 2.5 N.
steps: Fundamental on a wire fixed at both ends: wavelength = 2 x length = 2 x 0.187 = 0.374 m.
Wave speed v = f lambda, and tension T = v^2 mu = (f lambda)^2 mu.
Decrease in tension = T1 - T2 = 2.5 N.

questions.question: A laser, diffraction grating and screen are set up as shown. The position of the central maximum is O and the position of the first order maximum is X. The diffraction grating has 300 lines per mm. Which expression gives the wavelength of the laser light? A 300000 x (0.378/2.000); B 300000 x (0.378/2.035); C (1/300000) x (0.378/2.000); D (1/300000) x (0.378/2.035).
steps: The grating spacing is d = 1/300000 m (300 lines per mm = 300000 lines per m), so lambda = d sin theta with n = 1. This rules out A and B.
sin theta = opposite / hypotenuse. The sideways distance OX = 0.378 m is the opposite side and the slant distance from grating to X = 2.035 m is the hypotenuse.

questions.question: Two waves of wavelength lambda are produced by the same source. They travel different distances and meet, where the path difference is lambda/8. Which is the phase difference in radians? A pi/2; B pi/4; C pi/8; D pi/16.
questions.answer: B: pi / 4 radians.
steps: Phase difference = 2 pi x (path difference / lambda).
= 2 pi x (1/8) = pi / 4 rad.

questions.question: Two waves are coherent. Which must be true? A antiphase; B in phase; C same amplitude; D same frequency.
questions.answer: D - coherent waves must have the same frequency.
steps: Coherent waves have the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
They need not be in phase or antiphase, so A and B are not required.
Their amplitudes do not have to be equal, so C is not required.
The same frequency is required, so D is correct.

questions.question: This question refers to the standing wave pattern on a string as shown (loops VW, WX and XY). Which sections of the string would be in phase with each other? A VW and WX; B WX and XY; C VW and XY; D no sections are in phase.
questions.answer: C: VW and XY.
steps: In a standing wave, all points within one loop (between adjacent nodes) vibrate in phase.
Adjacent loops are in antiphase, so VW and WX are in antiphase, and so are WX and XY.
VW and XY are two loops apart (one wavelength), so they are in phase.

questions.question: Sound passes through gaps in metal plates about the wavelength in size. Walking along a line, the sound becomes quieter until no sound is heard. Explain this, referring to interference.
questions.answer: Waves from the gaps are coherent; as she walks the path differences change, and where they are odd multiples of half a wavelength the waves cancel, giving zero sound when the amplitudes are equal.
steps: Gaps of about one wavelength in size diffract the sound, so each gap acts as a secondary source.
The waves from the gaps come from one source, so they are coherent and interfere.
At X the path differences are zero or whole wavelengths, so the waves reinforce and the sound is loud.
As she walks along the line, the path differences from the gaps change steadily.
When the path difference is an odd multiple of lambda / 2, the waves arrive in antiphase and cancel (destructive interference).
With equal amplitudes from the gaps the resultant amplitude is zero, so no sound is heard.

questions.question: Two filament lamps on the same supply are used to try to produce a consistent interference pattern. Explain why this is not possible.
questions.answer: Filament lamps are independent, incoherent sources, so their phase difference changes randomly and no stable pattern forms.
steps: Each filament lamp emits light from many independent atomic emissions.
The waves from the two lamps have no fixed phase relationship, so they are not coherent.
The phase difference at any point changes rapidly and randomly.
So maxima and minima average out and no stable interference pattern is seen.

questions.question: In n = d sin theta for laser light through a grating, what does d represent? A spacing between adjacent lines; B grating-screen distance; C number of lines per metre; D order of the maximum.
questions.answer: A - the distance between adjacent lines (the grating spacing).
steps: In the grating equation n lambda = d sin theta, d is the grating spacing.
The grating spacing is the distance between adjacent lines or slits.
The grating-screen distance (B) is not the spacing d.
Lines per metre (C) is the reciprocal of d, and the order of maximum (D) is n.

questions.question: The formula for a diffraction grating in the list of equations is n lambda = d sin theta. Which of the following quantities does not have units? A n; B lambda; C d; D theta.
questions.answer: A: n.
steps: n is the order of the maximum, a pure number with no units.
lambda and d are lengths, measured in metres.
theta is an angle, measured in degrees (or radians), so it does have a unit. Only sin theta is unitless.

questions.question: A displacement-time graph for one point as a wave passes. Which statement is not correct? A period can be read; B wavelength can be read directly; C could be longitudinal; D could be transverse.
questions.answer: B - the wavelength cannot be read from a displacement-time graph; it gives the period.
steps: A displacement-time graph shows how one point oscillates against time.
The period, the time for one cycle, is read directly from it (A is correct).
Wavelength needs a displacement-distance graph, so B is not correct.
Whether the wave is longitudinal or transverse cannot be decided from this graph, so C and D are both possible.

questions.question: A string is placed under tension T. A wave travels along the string. A second string has the same mass but twice the length. A wave travels along it with the same velocity. Which is the tension in the second string? A 4T; B 2T; C T/2; D T/4.
steps: v = sqrt(T / mu), so T = mu v^2.
Mass per unit length mu = mass / length, so doubling the length at the same mass halves mu.
The speed v is the same, so the tension is also halved: T2 = (mu/2) v^2 = T / 2.

questions.question: Which statement about stationary waves is not correct? A points between adjacent nodes are in phase; B antinodes have maximum amplitude; C adjacent nodes are one wavelength apart; D no net energy transfer.
questions.answer: C - adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, not one wavelength.
steps: Adjacent nodes are separated by lambda / 2.
All points between two adjacent nodes move in phase (A is correct).
Antinodes are the points of maximum amplitude (B is correct).
A stationary wave transfers no net energy (D is correct), so C is the incorrect statement.

questions.question: Waves spread out as they pass an object. Which process is this? A diffraction; B interference; C reflection; D refraction.
questions.answer: A - diffraction.
steps: Waves spreading out after passing an object or gap is diffraction.
Interference is superposition of waves, not spreading.
Reflection is bouncing back off a surface.
Refraction is a change of direction on a change of speed.

questions.question: Two waves of wavelength 12 cm leave a source in phase. They travel along different paths to a point X. The path difference at X is 18 cm. Which is the phase difference between the two waves at X? A 0 radians; B pi/2 radians; C pi radians; D 3 pi/2 radians.
questions.answer: C: pi radians.
steps: Phase difference = 2 pi x (path difference / lambda) = 2 pi x 18/12 = 3 pi rad.
A phase difference of 3 pi is equivalent to pi once a whole cycle (2 pi) is subtracted, so the waves are in antiphase at X.
Of the options, only C (pi radians) matches.

questions.question: Laser light on a grating gives maxima on a screen. Which change decreases the distance between the central maximum and the first order? A decrease laser-grating distance; B increase grating-screen distance; C more lines per mm; D smaller wavelength.
questions.answer: D - using light of smaller wavelength decreases the separation.
steps: The separation of maxima on the screen is x = lambda D / d.
The laser-grating distance does not appear in the equation (A has no effect).
Increasing D increases x (B is wrong), and more lines per mm reduces d so increases x (C is wrong).
A smaller wavelength lambda reduces x, so D is correct.

questions.question: Explain how a standing wave can form on a cable fixed at both ends, driven by wind.
questions.answer: Waves reflect at the fixed ends and the incident and reflected waves superpose; when the length is a whole number of half wavelengths, nodes form at the ends and antinodes between.
steps: Wind makes the cable vibrate, sending transverse waves along it.
The waves reflect at both fixed ends, so waves travel in both directions.
Incident and reflected waves of the same frequency and amplitude superpose.
Where they are always in antiphase there are nodes; where they are in phase there are antinodes.
A standing wave forms when the cable length is a whole number of half wavelengths.

questions.question: A standing wave on a cable fixed at both ends, with two points X and Y marked on the diagram. Answer the part about X and Y.
questions.answer: Part (b) has no instruction on the page (only the diagram and the statement that X and Y are two points on the cable), so what to answer cannot be determined.

questions.question: A suspending cable has mass 2.10 x 10^3 kg and length 87.0 m. Show that the mass per unit length is about 24 kg m-1.
questions.answer: mu = 2.10 x 10^3 kg / 87.0 m = 24.1 kg m-1, which is about 24 kg m-1.
steps: Mass per unit length mu = total mass / length.
mu = 24.1 kg m-1, which rounds to about 24 kg m-1 as required.
Check the units: kg divided by m gives kg m-1, as required.

questions.question: Lowest humming frequency is 280 Hz. Road mass 140 x 10^6 kg is supported equally by 500 cables of lengths 3.5 m to 160 m, mu = 24 kg m-1. Deduce whether the lowest-frequency standing waves on the cables could produce the hum.
questions.answer: No. The lowest (fundamental) frequencies of the cables lie between about 1 Hz and 48 Hz, so none can give 280 Hz.
steps: Tension in each cable: T = (140 x 10^6 kg / 500) x 9.81 = 2.75 x 10^6 N.
Wave speed on each cable: v = sqrt(T / mu) = sqrt(2.75 x 10^6 / 24) = 338 m s-1.
The lowest standing wave on a cable fixed at both ends has f = v / (2L).
Longest cable (160 m): f = 338 / 320 = 1.06 Hz; shortest cable (3.5 m): f = 338 / 7.0 = 48.3 Hz.
So the lowest frequencies of all the cables lie between about 1 Hz and 48 Hz.
280 Hz is outside this range, so the lowest-frequency standing waves cannot produce the hum.

questions.question: State what is meant by a transverse wave.
questions.answer: A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
steps: In a transverse wave the particles or fields oscillate.
The oscillations are at right angles to the direction in which the wave transfers energy.
Light is transverse because its electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to its direction of travel.
Unlike a longitudinal wave, the oscillations are not along the direction of travel.

questions.question: A laser beam is split into two paths that reach a photographic film. Explain how light from the two paths could cause constructive interference.
questions.answer: The two beams are coherent (from one laser); where their path difference is a whole number of wavelengths they arrive in phase and reinforce.
steps: The beam splitter divides one laser beam, so the two beams are coherent with a constant phase difference.
At points on the film where the path lengths differ by a whole number of wavelengths, the waves are in phase.
In-phase waves superpose constructively, so the amplitude and intensity increase there.
These bright regions are recorded on the film, forming the interference pattern.

questions.question: Oscilloscope trace of a pipe sound with time base 1 division = 1.5 ms. Calculate the frequency.
questions.answer: Frequency = 4.1 x 10^2 Hz (about 410 Hz).
steps: Measure over many cycles to be accurate: the trace shows 6 complete cycles between the first and the last peak.
6 cycles take about 9.8 divisions, so the period is T = 9.8 / 6 = 1.63 divisions.

questions.question: Wave 1 and wave 2 in the same pipe (open top, closed bottom) are shown with nodes and antinodes. Explain how the frequency of wave 1 compares with wave 2.
questions.answer: The frequency of wave 2 is three times the frequency of wave 1 (wave 1 has one third the frequency of wave 2).
steps: Both waves have a node at the closed bottom and an antinode at the open top, in the same pipe of length L, and sound travels at the same speed v in both.
Wave 1: node to the next antinode is lambda / 4, so L = lambda1 / 4 and lambda1 = 4L.
Wave 2: node, antinode, node, antinode is three quarter-wavelengths, so L = 3 lambda2 / 4 and lambda2 = 4L / 3.
v = f lambda with the same v, so f is inversely proportional to lambda: f2 / f1 = lambda1 / lambda2 = 3.

questions.question: The student plotted frequency and wavelength of sound from different pipes. Determine a value for the speed of sound from the graph.
questions.answer: Speed of sound = about 3.3 x 10^2 m s^-1 (the gradient of the graph).
steps: v = f lambda, so lambda = v x (1/f): the gradient of wavelength against 1/frequency is the speed of sound.
Draw a best-fit line and read two well-separated points, for example (0.00105 Hz^-1, 0.335 m) and (0.00150 Hz^-1, 0.485 m).

questions.question: Speed of sound is 340 m s-1. The stationary wave in the longest pipe (length 28.2 cm, open at top, closed at bottom) is produced. Determine its frequency.
questions.answer: Frequency = 301 Hz (simplest mode, lambda = 4L).
steps: The pipe is closed at one end and open at the other, so the simplest stationary wave has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.
This is a quarter wavelength in the pipe: L = lambda / 4, so lambda = 4 L = 4 x 0.282 = 1.128 m.
This assumes the simplest (fundamental) mode, as the question describes the simplest stationary wave in the longest pipe.

questions.question: Give one safety precaution for the laser diffraction grating experiment.
questions.answer: Do not look directly into the laser beam or its reflections (use eye protection and keep the beam away from eyes).
steps: Laser light is intense and concentrated, and can damage the retina.
Never look directly into the beam or at reflections from shiny surfaces.
Keep the beam at a height away from people's eyes and use eye protection where appropriate.
Laser safety rules apply even though the beam is low power.

questions.question: State what measurements the student should make to determine the wavelength of the laser light.
questions.answer: The grating-to-screen distance L and the distance x from the central maximum to the first order maximum.
steps: Use lambda = d x / L, from the grating equation for small angles.
Measure the grating-to-screen distance L with a metre rule.
Measure the distance x from the central maximum to the first order maximum on the screen.
Use d = 1 / 250 mm, the known grating spacing, to find lambda.

questions.question: Two first order maxima are 18 deg apart with a grating of 250 lines per mm. Show that the wavelength is about 600 nm.
questions.answer: lambda = d sin theta = 4.0 x 10^-6 m x sin 9.0 deg = 6.3 x 10^-7 m (626 nm), about 600 nm.
steps: Grating spacing d = 1 / 250 mm = 4.0 x 10^-3 mm = 4.0 x 10^-6 m.
The two first order maxima are symmetric about the centre, so each is at theta = 18 / 2 = 9.0 deg.
Grating equation for first order: lambda = d sin theta = 4.0 x 10^-6 x sin 9.0 deg.
sin 9.0 deg = 0.1564, so lambda = 6.26 x 10^-7 m = 626 nm, which rounds to about 600 nm.

questions.question: Using the same grating and laser, determine the greatest order of maximum the student could observe.
steps: The largest possible angle has sin theta = 1, so n lambda / d must be at most 1.
n is at most d / lambda = 4.0 x 10^-6 / 6.26 x 10^-7 = 6.4.
The greatest whole-number order is n = 6 (check: sin theta = 6 x 626 / 4000 = 0.94, which is valid).
A seventh order would need sin theta above 1, so it cannot be seen.

questions.question: In a white light spectrum from a grating, explain why violet light is closest to the central maximum.
questions.answer: Violet has the shortest wavelength, so for a given order its diffraction angle (sin theta = n lambda / d) is the smallest.
steps: For a given order n, sin theta = n lambda / d.
Violet light has the shortest wavelength of visible light.
So sin theta, and therefore theta, is smallest for violet.
Violet is therefore closest to the central maximum.

questions.question: The grating has line spacing 1.62 x 10^-6 m. Calculate the wavelength of the violet light.
questions.answer: Wavelength of the violet light = 3.9 x 10^-7 m (392 nm).
steps: The diagram shows the first-order spectrum, with the violet edge at theta = 14 deg to the central line.
n lambda = d sin theta with n = 1.
lambda = 3.92 x 10^-7 m, about 390 nm, a violet wavelength.

questions.question: Describe how Huygens construction can be used to predict the shape of diffracted wavefronts.
questions.answer: Treat each point on the incoming wavefront at the gap as a source of circular wavelets; the common tangent (envelope) of these wavelets is the new wavefront.
steps: Mark a series of points along the incoming wavefront at the gap.
From each point draw a circle (wavelet) whose radius is the wave speed times the time interval.
Draw the envelope, the common tangent to all the wavelets; this is the new wavefront.
For a narrow gap the new wavefronts beyond it are approximately semicircular.

questions.question: Waves arrive parallel to the harbour wall through two gaps, with varying wavelength. Explain why the boat at A always oscillates strongly and the boat at B oscillates strongly or very weakly depending on wavelength.
questions.answer: A is on the axis midway between the two gaps, so the waves from the gaps always arrive in phase and A is always a maximum. B is off-axis, so the path difference depends on the wavelength: whole number of wavelengths gives a large amplitude and an odd number of half wavelengths gives a very small amplitude.
steps: The gaps are comparable to the wavelength, so the waves diffract and spread into the harbour. The two gaps are in the same wavefront, so they act as coherent sources in phase, and the waves from them overlap and superpose.
A lies on the line of symmetry midway between the gaps, so the path lengths from the two gaps are equal.
The path difference at A is zero for every wavelength, so the waves always arrive in phase: constructive interference and always a large amplitude.
B is closer to one gap than the other, so there is a fixed non-zero path difference, but its value in wavelengths changes as the wavelength changes.
When the path difference at B is a whole number of wavelengths, the waves are in phase: constructive interference and a large amplitude.
When the path difference at B is an odd number of half wavelengths, the waves are in antiphase: destructive interference and almost no oscillation.

questions.question: There is tension T in a string of length l. When the string is displaced and then released, waves move on the string with speed v. A string of length 2l has the same diameter and is made from the same material. The tension in this string is 2T. Which expression gives the speed of waves on the string of length 2l? A v/sqrt(2); B v/2; C sqrt(2) v; D 2v.
questions.answer: C: sqrt(2) v.
steps: v = sqrt(T / mu). The mass per unit length mu = density x cross-sectional area, which is the same for both strings (same material and diameter), whatever their lengths.
The new tension is 2T with the same mu, so v_new = sqrt(2T / mu) = sqrt(2) x sqrt(T / mu) = sqrt(2) v.

questions.question: State what is meant by a transverse wave, for waves travelling along a harp string.
questions.answer: A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
steps: In a transverse wave the string moves up and down or side to side.
The motion is at right angles to the direction the wave carries energy along the string.
This is what distinguishes a transverse wave from a longitudinal one.
Example: each point on the string moves up and down while the wave travels along the string.

questions.question: A harp string fixed at both ends vibrates at its lowest frequency. Describe the stationary wave to be added to the diagram, labelling nodes and antinodes.
questions.answer: A single loop: nodes at both fixed ends and one antinode at the centre of the string.
steps: Both fixed ends must be nodes, since the string cannot move there.
The lowest frequency has the longest wavelength, so the string length equals lambda / 2.
This gives one antinode in the centre between the two nodes.
Mark a node at each fixed end and one antinode at the centre.

questions.question: String produces 196 Hz with wavelength 0.72 m under tension 41 N. Deduce which new string (A, B, C or D, of given masses for 1.5 m) should replace it, cut to the same length.
questions.answer: String B.
steps: Wave speed v = f lambda = 196 Hz x 0.72 m = 141 m s^-1.
The new string has the same tension and must give the same wave speed, so it needs the same mass per unit length. This does not depend on how much is cut off.
String B (3.1 g in 1.5 m) matches the required 2.06 x 10^-3 kg m^-1.

questions.question: Light from a laser is coherent. State what is meant by coherent.
questions.answer: Waves have the same frequency (wavelength) and a constant phase difference between them.
steps: Coherent waves have the same frequency.
They also maintain a constant phase difference over time.
Only coherent waves produce stable interference patterns.
Because the laser light is coherent, the incident and reflected light can interfere.

questions.question: Laser light is incident at 90 deg on a reflective surface. State why a standing wave forms between the laser and the surface.
questions.answer: The incident and reflected waves have the same frequency and travel in opposite directions, so they superpose to form a standing wave.
steps: Light travels from the laser to the surface and is reflected straight back along the same path.
The incident and reflected waves have the same frequency and travel in opposite directions.
They superpose, forming nodes and antinodes at fixed positions.
The reflected wave returns along the same path, so the two waves are exactly opposed in direction.

questions.question: Describe how a stationary wave is formed inside a tube closed at one end, with a vibrating tuning fork near the open end.
questions.answer: Sound from the fork travels into the tube, reflects at the closed end and superposes with the incident wave; resonance gives a stationary wave with a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.
steps: The tuning fork produces longitudinal sound waves that enter the tube through the open end.
The waves travel down the tube and reflect at the closed end, where the air cannot move, so it is a displacement node.
Incident and reflected waves of the same frequency and amplitude superpose in opposite directions.
At the open end the air can move freely, so there is an antinode there.
The waves reinforce when the tube length is an odd number of quarter wavelengths: L = (2n - 1) lambda / 4.
At this resonant frequency the air column vibrates strongly in a stationary wave and the sound is loud.

questions.question: Tube length 20.4 cm gives the simplest stationary wave; speed of sound 340 m s-1. Calculate the frequency of the sound produced.
questions.answer: Frequency = 417 Hz.
steps: The simplest stationary wave in a tube closed at one end has L = lambda / 4.
Use consistent SI units, with L converted to metres (0.204 m).

questions.question: The actual frequency of the tube sound is slightly less than the calculated value. Suggest why.
questions.answer: The antinode at the open end lies slightly outside the tube, so the effective length is longer than 20.4 cm, which lowers the frequency.
steps: At the open end the antinode does not form exactly at the physical end of the tube.
The effective acoustic length of the air column is slightly longer than the physical length.
Using this longer length in f = v / (4L) gives a lower frequency than the calculated value.
This end correction makes the tube sound at a slightly lower pitch than calculated.

questions.question: Light is a transverse wave. State what is meant by a transverse wave.
questions.answer: A wave whose oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
steps: In a transverse wave the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of travel.
Energy is transferred along the direction of travel of the wave.
Polarisation is possible only for transverse waves.
Light waves in a vacuum travel at 3.00 x 10^8 m s-1.

questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength 650 nm; screen distance L = 1.30 m; distance from central maximum to first order x = 0.22 m. Calculate the number of lines per mm on the grating.
questions.answer: About 257 lines per mm (d = 3.90 x 10^-6 m).
steps: For the first order, d sin theta = lambda, with lambda = 650 x 10^-9 m.
From the geometry, tan theta = x / L = 0.22 / 1.30 = 0.169, so theta = 9.61 deg.
sin theta = 0.1669.
Lines per mm = 1 / (3.895 x 10^-3 mm) = 257 lines per mm.

questions.question: Explain how a first order maximum is produced on the screen.
questions.answer: Light diffracts at each line; at the first order angle the path difference between neighbouring lines is one wavelength, so the waves are in phase and interfere constructively.
steps: Each line of the grating diffracts the coherent laser light in many directions.
At the first order angle, the path difference between waves from adjacent lines is exactly one wavelength.
Waves from all the lines are therefore in phase at this angle and reinforce.
This gives a bright first order maximum where d sin theta = lambda.

questions.question: Two waves, of wavelength 2 m, are produced by a source at point X. Both waves are initially in phase. The waves travel different distances and meet at point Y: the upper route is 4 m + 4 m and the lower route is 3 m + 6 m. Which is the phase difference, in radians, between the two waves at point Y? A 0; B pi/4; C pi/2; D pi.
questions.answer: D: pi radians.
steps: Upper route = 4 + 4 = 8 m. Lower route = 3 + 6 = 9 m.
Path difference = 1 m = lambda / 2 (lambda = 2 m).
Phase difference = 2 pi x (1/2) = pi rad: the waves arrive in antiphase.

questions.question: A plucked string of frequency f in an apparatus. Which single change would increase f? A decrease length l; B decrease mass m; C increase cross-sectional area; D increase mass per unit length.
questions.answer: A - decreasing the length l increases the frequency.
steps: The fundamental frequency of a string fixed at both ends is f = (1 / 2l) sqrt(T / mu).
Decreasing the length l increases f, so A is correct.
Decreasing the hanging mass m reduces the tension T and so reduces f (B is wrong).
Increasing the cross-sectional area or the mass per unit length mu reduces f (C and D are wrong).

questions.question: Two waves on a string move towards each other at the same speed and with the same wavelength. The diagram shows the string when the waves are half a wavelength apart (each wave is a crest followed by a trough, with the troughs leading). Which of the diagrams A to D shows the string when both waves have moved a distance of half a wavelength?
questions.answer: B: a crest, then a deep trough (twice as deep), then a crest.
steps: Each wave is one wavelength long (a crest and a trough), and the two leading troughs face each other.
The gap between the waves is half a wavelength. When each wave moves half a wavelength, the two waves overlap over half a wavelength: the leading trough of each wave.
Where they overlap, the two troughs add (principle of superposition) to give one trough with twice the depth.
On either side the remaining crests of each wave are unaffected, so the shape is crest, double-depth trough, crest, which is B.

questions.question: Label each node N and each antinode A on the standing wave shown.
questions.answer: N at each end of the string (two nodes) and A at the middle of the loop (one antinode).
steps: The string is fixed (or cannot move) at both ends, so there are nodes (N) at both ends.
The single loop shows the fundamental mode, so the point of maximum amplitude in the middle is the only antinode (A).

questions.question: Explain how a standing wave forms on the vibrating string.
questions.answer: Incident and reflected waves of equal frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions superpose; nodes are where they cancel and antinodes where they reinforce.
steps: The vibration generator sends transverse waves along the string.
The waves reflect at the fixed support, so waves travel in both directions.
Incident and reflected waves of equal frequency and amplitude superpose.
Points where they are always in antiphase are nodes, with zero displacement; points in phase are antinodes, with maximum amplitude.
A standing wave forms when the string length is a whole number of half wavelengths.

questions.question: Explain why the graph of f squared against T is a straight line with gradient 1 / (4 l^2 mu) (same mode and length l).
questions.answer: f^2 = (n^2 / 4 l^2 mu) T, so f^2 is directly proportional to T; the line passes through the origin and its gradient is n^2 / (4 l^2 mu), a constant for fixed mode, length and mu.
steps: For the same shape of standing wave the mode n and length l are fixed.
Wave speed v = sqrt(T / mu), and v = f lambda with lambda = 2l / n.
So f = (n / 2l) sqrt(T / mu), and squaring gives f^2 = (n^2 / 4 l^2 mu) T.
Since l, mu and n are constant, f^2 is directly proportional to T, giving a straight line through the origin.

questions.topic: Mass per Unit Length from Graph
questions.question: Using the student's graph of f squared against T with l = 0.85 m, determine the mass per unit length mu of the string.
steps: The graph is a straight line through the origin, so the gradient is f^2 / T = 1 / (4 l^2 mu).
Using the best-fit line, for example the point (5.0 N, 2650 Hz^2): gradient = 2650 / 5.0 = 5.3 x 10^2 Hz^2 N^-1.

questions.question: The diagram shows a wave of amplitude A on a string. P and Q are two points on the string (either side of the crest). The wave on the string is a stationary wave. Which row is correct? Phase difference between P and Q / amplitude of oscillation of P and Q: A 0 deg, equal to A; B 0 deg, less than A; C 90 deg, equal to A; D 90 deg, less than A.
questions.answer: B: phase difference 0 deg, amplitude less than A.
steps: P and Q are on the same loop, between the same pair of nodes, so they vibrate in phase: phase difference 0 deg (not 90 deg).
In a stationary wave the amplitude varies with position. Only the antinode at the crest has amplitude A.
P and Q are away from the antinode, so each has amplitude less than A.
